q: Does MLE-QAE extend cleanly to multi-amplitude / multi-variable estimation, where the good-subspace is not 2-D but a superposition over several tagged outcomes?
basis: Paper is restricted to a single scalar amplitude a in [0,1]. Real Monte Carlo integration and option-pricing pipelines often need joint estimation of several amplitudes (e.g. tranched expectations, delta/gamma sensitivities). It is not obvious the closed-form product-likelihood factorization survives when good/bad splits into K>2 mutually exclusive outcomes with their own m_k-dependent probabilities.
next_steps: 1) Derive the K-outcome joint likelihood analytically; check whether the block-diagonal Grover-rotation structure gives a tractable factorization. 2) Implement a 3-amplitude simulator on the classical-statevector side (still no qubit sim needed) and measure whether the per-amplitude CRB is saturated by a joint MLE. 3) Compare against running K independent MLE-QAE runs to quantify the sample-cost savings from jointness.

q: How does MLE-QAE integrate with modern error mitigation (ZNE, PEC, virtual distillation) on NISQ hardware, and does mitigation preserve the near-Heisenberg scaling or degrade it back toward classical N^{-1/2}?
basis: Paper is entirely noiseless / classical statevector. Depolarizing or gate-error noise on Q^{m_k} damps the sin^2((2m+1)theta) signal exponentially in m, which is exactly the regime where EIS gets its advantage. Error mitigation typically inflates variance in a way that may collapse the m-dependent Fisher information gain.
next_steps: 1) Add a per-gate depolarizing-noise model to the good-subspace simulator; measure the effective information vs m curve. 2) Overlay a ZNE-style noise-scaled sweep and refit the MLE; check whether the fitted slope stays below -0.75 or reverts to -0.5. 3) Compare against a virtual-distillation post-processing on the same shots.

q: For the paper's own headline application (Monte Carlo option pricing / European-call expectation values), what is the empirical MSE-vs-total-queries curve for MLE-QAE against a fully-classical QMC baseline, at industrially-relevant precision targets (e.g. 1e-4 relative)?
basis: Sec. 4 of the paper reports CNOT counts, not end-to-end MSE-vs-queries against a classical baseline. The MLE-QAE quantum-advantage argument only closes if the (quantum queries) crossover with classical QMC actually lands at a useful precision, not just in the asymptotic scaling.
next_steps: 1) Wire the MLE-QAE post-processor to a small European-call payoff loaded via a standard quantum-arithmetic block (still simulated classically). 2) Run both MLE-QAE and vanilla classical Monte Carlo to matched target-MSE and plot query-counts. 3) Report the crossover precision at which quantum queries beat classical samples, and whether it lies below or above the 1e-4 relative-error target typical for pricing.

q: How robust is the maximum-likelihood post-processing itself when the assumed likelihood model is misspecified by realistic hardware effects (readout bias, mid-circuit leakage, drift)?
basis: The paper's likelihood L_k assumes P(good) = sin^2((2m_k+1)theta) exactly. On real devices this is off by readout-confusion, per-gate coherent errors, and shot-to-shot drift. It is unknown at what scale of model-mismatch the MLE loses its unbiasedness or its CRB saturation.
next_steps: 1) Perturb the simulator's forward model with a readout-confusion matrix and a coherent over-rotation per Q application; keep the MLE using the ideal likelihood. 2) Sweep magnitude of the perturbation and measure bias(a_hat), RMSE/CRB. 3) Test whether a data-augmented MLE (fit theta AND a readout-bias nuisance jointly) restores unbiasedness.

q: Does an adaptive Bayesian / online schedule for {m_k} beat the fixed EIS schedule at matched query budget, particularly in the low-shot regime where finite-N_shot bias currently makes the empirical slope shallower than -0.95?
basis: The paper uses hand-crafted classical / LIS / EIS schedules. It is plausible that a Bayesian scheduler that picks the next m_k to maximize expected Fisher-information gain given the current posterior on theta would close the gap between measured slope (-0.866 in our replication, -0.95 in the paper) and the Heisenberg limit -1.0, and would do so with fewer total queries at moderate precision targets.
next_steps: 1) Implement a Bayesian MLE-QAE loop: after each Q^{m_k} batch, update posterior on theta, then pick m_{k+1} = argmax expected Fisher info under posterior. 2) Compare RMSE-vs-N_q against EIS at N_shot = 100, 1000 to see if the adaptive schedule removes the finite-shot slope deficit. 3) Report query-budget savings at fixed 1e-5 relative precision target.
